title_en: Ramtin Naimi - The State of Venture - [Invest Like the Best, EP.499]
title_zh: Abstract Ventures 的 Ramtin Naimi 谈风险投资现状（The State of Venture）
subtitle_zh: 种子投资人 Ramtin Naimi 拆解当下 VC 市场的疯狂节奏、算力融资、LP 困境与估值泡沫。
summary_zh: 本期 Invest Like the Best 由 Patrick O'Shaughnessy 对话 Abstract Ventures 的种子投资人 Ramtin Naimi，聚焦「风险投资现状」（the state of venture），刻意不谈宏大叙事，而是落到旧金山一笔笔交易的层面。Naimi 形容当下节奏「快得离谱」：融资轮与后续轮（follow-on round）都比以往更快发生，少数顶级机构能拿到优惠定价的第一档（tranche number one），而错过交易的 VC 不再甘于「维持关系、等下一轮」，而是当场挤进本轮，代价常是 3 倍、4 倍甚至 5 倍估值——这就是二级档（secondary tranche），硅谷戏称「绿帽档」（Cuck tranche）。他并不认为分档（tranching）是市场不健康的信号，反而是资本密集型公司的必需品，并直言「谁说自己从没被绿过都是在扯淡」。他提醒市场里误导人之处：一些年增 10 到 20 倍的公司，其营收并非干净的高毛利、年度经常性收入（ARR）合同制 SaaS 营收。节目还谈到 LP 侧与募资的错配（承诺资本需数周才能到位）、SpaceX/Anthropic/OpenAI 三家万亿美元公司如何重塑估值动态、种子基金规模从 2018 年 1 亿被嫌大、到 2026 年 8 亿被赞「有纪律」的反转，以及他对物理智能（physical intelligence）与留人能力的看好。

turns.en: One of our mutual p's describes you as the person from whom he learns the most per minute about what's going on in venture markets when he talks to you. We're trying to recreate that here today and really focus on not big picture stuff, the history of abstract, etc. We did the first time, but really just zoom in on this moment in time.
turns.zh: 我们的一位共同 LP 形容你是这样一个人：每次和你聊完，他从你这里每分钟了解到的风险投资市场动态是最多的。我们今天想在这儿重现那种感觉，真正聚焦的不是宏大叙事、也不是 Abstract 的历史等等——那些我们第一次已经聊过了——而是真正聚焦当下这个时间点。

turns.en: How would you describe the state of things right now, like zoomed all the way into the deal level here around San Francisco? It's very fast paced, insanely fast paced, in the sense that rounds are happening quicker than ever. Follow on rounds are happening quicker than ever.
turns.zh: 你会怎么形容现在这种状态？就是聚焦到旧金山这边一笔笔交易的层面？节奏非常快，快得离谱，意思是融资轮发生得比以往任何时候都快，后续轮（follow-on round）也发生得比以往任何时候都快。

turns.en: There are certain companies that just get a lot of attention very early in their life cycle. And they get a lot of demand for their financing, whether it's their seat or their series A or their series B.
turns.zh: 有一些公司在它们生命周期非常早的阶段就会获得大量关注，市场对它们融资的需求很大，无论是种子轮（seed）、A 轮（Series A）还是 B 轮（Series B）。

turns.en: There is a handful of firms that those founders want to raise capital from and those guys get preferential pricing, which is really branch number one. And there's a bunch of VC firms that lose that deal. And historically, the VC firms that lost the deal would say, okay, we'll maintain a relationship.
turns.zh: 有那么一小撮机构，是这些创始人想要从其手中融资的，而这些机构能拿到优惠定价，这就是所谓的第一档（tranche number one）。还有一大堆 VC 机构错过了那笔交易。而在过去，错过交易的 VC 机构会说，好，我们会维持这段关系。

turns.en: We'll put in a small check or something to maintain that relationship. And as the thing performs, we'll do the next round. And in 2021, you have the fast follow, which was a couple of weeks later, they would raise a 2x evaluation from one of the people that lost that financing.
turns.zh: 我们会开一张小额支票之类的来维持关系，等这家公司表现出来了，我们再投下一轮。而在 2021 年，你会看到快速跟投（fast follow），也就是几周之后，他们会以两倍估值从当初错过那轮融资的人手里融到钱。

turns.en: But in this market, it's like, okay, we lost this round, but we don't want to wait for the next round. What do we need to pay to get into this financing today? And it's usually not 2x, it's usually like 3 to 4 to 5x happening in tandem with the primary.
turns.zh: 但在当前这个市场，情况变成了：好，我们错过了这一轮，但我们不想等到下一轮。今天要挤进这轮融资，我们需要付出什么代价？而这个代价通常不是 2 倍，通常是 3 倍、4 倍、5 倍，而且是与主轮（primary）同步发生的。

turns.en: And that's the secondary tronch, which has become known elegantly in Silicon Valley as the Cuck tronch. But the thing that's interesting is these companies are so capital intensive that they actually need that level of capital. And they don't want to raise all that in that primary tronch.
turns.zh: 这就是二级档（secondary tranche），在硅谷它有了一个优雅的别称，叫绿帽档（Cuck tranche）。但有意思的地方在于，这些公司资本密集度太高了，它们确实需要那么大量的资本，而它们又不想把所有这些钱都放在主档里融。

turns.en: So I don't think that tronching is a thing that's an unhealthy sign of the market. I think it's actually a necessity of these types of companies and the environment that we're in. Sometimes you get into the early tronch, you know, if you will get into the second tronch, and sometimes you're the one getting cuck.
turns.zh: 所以我不认为分档（tranching）是市场不健康的信号。我觉得它其实是这类公司、以及我们所处环境的必需品。有时候你能进早期档，或者说进第二档，而有时候你才是那个被戴绿帽的人。

turns.en: I think anybody who tells you they've never gotten cucked is completely bullshit. Everyone's gotten cucked once or twice at least. And anyone who says otherwise is lying to you. Things like that are happening. You're also having people running around like chickens their heads cut off trying to just keep up with the market.
turns.zh: 我觉得任何说自己从没被绿过的人，完全是在扯淡。每个人至少都被绿过一两次，谁要说没有，那就是在骗你。诸如此类的事情正在发生。你还会看到一些人像没头苍蝇一样到处乱窜，只想跟上市场节奏。

turns.en: Throwing out offers very, very quickly. And then you're also seeing some bad behavior where people are changing those offers quickly after the fact or pulling those offers. A lot of things that are somewhat reminiscent of 2021 in that sense.
turns.zh: 非常非常快地甩出报价。然后你还会看到一些恶劣行为，比如有人在事后很快更改报价，或者直接撤回报价。很多这类情况在某种意义上让人联想到 2021 年。

turns.en: But the other things you're seeing is the pace at which things are moving kind of makes everyone feel like they need to do something to stay ahead of the curve. When this market getting markups is the bare minimum requirement to be keeping up. So the point where markups don't even feel like good anymore.
turns.zh: 但你看到的另一件事是，事情推进的速度让每个人都觉得自己必须做点什么才能保持领先。在当前这个市场，拿到 markup（估值上调）只是跟上节奏的最低要求，以至于 markup 都不再让人觉得是好事了。

turns.en: Markups just feel like you're keeping pace with the state of the market. Once every three weeks, you have something happen in your portfolio that makes you feel pretty good. And you're like, okay, cool, I'm doing really, really well in this market. Then the subsequent three weeks, you see things happen to companies that you're not in.
turns.zh: markup 只是让你感觉跟上了市场的步伐。每隔三周，你的组合里就会有件事发生，让你感觉相当不错，你会想，好，酷，我在这个市场里做得真的非常好。然后接下来的三周，你又看到一些你没投的公司发生了大事。

turns.en: Then you're like, holy shit, I'm falling behind once again. You see the pace at which things are happening. You're seeing exits that are the largest in history happen. And then it's news for like two days and people move on to the next thing. So I'd say the pace at which things are happening is not unprecedented.
turns.zh: 然后你就想，天呐，我又落后了。你能看到事情发生的速度，你会看到史上最大规模的退出（exit）发生，然后它成为新闻也就两天，人们就转向下一件事了。所以我要说，事情发生的这个速度并非史无前例。

turns.en: Because I think the similar pace happened in 2021. I think the pace is more healthy today because you know, there's real value creation. These companies are doing truly amazing things. I do think the thing that's a little misleading about this market is the story behind the revenue with all these companies.
turns.zh: 因为我觉得类似的速度在 2021 年就出现过。我认为今天的节奏更健康，因为这里有真实的价值创造，这些公司在做真正了不起的事情。我确实觉得这个市场里有点误导人的地方，是这些公司营收背后的故事。

turns.en: You do have companies growing 10, 15, 20 X year over year. But I think any company that's growing at that rate has something interesting about their revenue. It's not a clear clean pure play SaaS revenue and 90% plus gross margins annualized recurring revenue contracts.
turns.zh: 你确实有一些公司每年同比增长 10 倍、15 倍、20 倍。但我认为任何以这种速度增长的公司，其营收里都有点耐人寻味的东西。那不是干净纯粹的 SaaS 营收，不是那种毛利率 90% 以上、年度经常性收入（ARR）合同制的营收。

turns.en: They all have something that's either ridiculously high growth but very low margins. Either low margins or negative margins, ridiculously fast growth but really high customer concentration or annualizing revenue because they're selling data and whatever their revenue was last month.
turns.zh: 它们都有那么点东西：要么增长快得离谱但利润率很低——低利润率甚至负利润率；要么增长极快但客户集中度非常高；要么是把营收年化——因为它们在卖数据，上个月营收是多少，

turns.en: They multiply by 12 and that's their annualized revenue or its consumer based revenue and not enterprise based revenue or its usage based revenue and not contractual rate. So there's a lot of that. And I think that could be somewhat discouraging the founders whose companies aren't growing that pace when they see those numbers.
turns.zh: 他们就乘以 12，那就是它们的年化营收；要么是面向消费者的营收而非企业级营收；要么是按用量计费（usage-based）的营收而非合同制营收。所以这类情况很多。我觉得当那些公司增速没那么快的创始人看到这些数字时，这可能会有点打击他们。

turns.en: And they think like, oh my god, I'm completely left behind. But I think if you peel back the layers and you start looking at it, you need to actually compare your revenue growth to companies within your style of company versus the absolute top line figures.
turns.zh: 他们会想，天呐，我彻底被甩在后面了。但我觉得如果你层层剥开、开始细看，你其实需要把自己的营收增长跟同类风格的公司去比，而不是去比那些绝对的收入顶端数字。

turns.en: You have data labeling company is growing in insane rates with their margins or 15 to 20% because getting that data is expensive. You have other companies that are reliant on foundation model providers to power their products and all of the margin goes to the foundation model companies.
turns.zh: 你会有数据标注公司以疯狂的增速增长，但利润率只有 15% 到 20%，因为获取那些数据成本很高。你还有其他公司依赖基础模型（foundation model）提供商来驱动它们的产品，结果所有利润都流向了基础模型公司。

turns.en: But the cool thing that you are seeing is that these margins are improving a really rapid clips and tropics were 85% in the first half of this year. They said, we have companies in our portfolio that are going to grow 200 to 700 this year, but their margin profiles are going from negative 15% to positive 35%.
turns.zh: 但你看到的很酷的一点是，这些利润率正在以非常快的速度改善。Anthropic 今年上半年是 85%，他们说我们组合里有些公司今年会增长 200% 到 700%，而它们的利润率画像正从负 15% 升到正 35%。

turns.en: So you're getting massive revenue growth and margin growth simultaneously. And then you have other companies that are like vertical SaaS businesses that are getting 100x revenue multiples.
turns.zh: 所以你会同时看到营收的大幅增长和利润率的大幅提升。然后你还有其他一些公司，它们像是垂直 SaaS（vertical SaaS）业务，却拿到了 100 倍的收入倍数。

turns.en: And then you look at that and people like, well, how do you compare that to the public markets when the SaaS multiples publicly or at 13X revenue multiples. And you look at these and you're like, well, are these actually SaaS businesses or these labor replacement businesses?
turns.zh: 然后你看着这个，人们会问，那你怎么把它跟公开市场比？公开市场上 SaaS 的倍数是 13 倍收入。你看这些公司，就会想，它们到底算不算 SaaS 业务，还是说它们是劳动力替代（labor replacement）业务？

turns.en: And then some people don't buy the labor replacement thesis, but the way you actually kind of have to believe in it is these companies are still growing 5, 7, 10, X year over year, even at like the massive scale they're already at.
turns.zh: 然后有些人不买劳动力替代这套论点，但你真正要去相信它的方式是：这些公司即便已经到了如此庞大的规模，仍然在以每年 5 倍、7 倍、10 倍的速度增长。

turns.en: I haven't seen them actually start to replace labor yet, but the pace at which they're growing, you know, if you look at companies that sell to law firms, you look at the total amount of money that law firms spend on software every year.
turns.zh: 我还没看到它们真正开始替代劳动力，但看它们增长的速度——你知道，如果你去看那些卖给律师事务所的公司，去看看律师事务所每年在软件上花的总金额，

turns.en: And you're like, oh, these companies can't be that big actually, but you look at how much money that these law firms spend on parolegals every year. And you're like, oh, that's actually really big number. So if these companies can capture 20% of that, the scale or the math starts to really, really work.
turns.zh: 你会想，哦，这些公司其实做不到那么大。但你再看看这些律所每年花在律师助理（paralegal）上的钱，你会想，哦，那其实是个非常大的数字。所以如果这些公司能拿下其中的 20%，这个规模、这笔账就真的非常成立了。

turns.en: If you were to compare this to 2021, which you lived through and were very active through, obviously two very euphoric, frothy-seeming markets, what are the most notable differences in similarities?
turns.zh: 如果拿这个跟 2021 年比——你亲历了那段时期、并且在其中非常活跃——显然是两个都非常亢奋、看起来都很泡沫化的市场，那么最显著的差异和相似之处是什么？

turns.en: If you look back to 2021, the companies weren't that interesting when you looked at them, which is we didn't have anything else to compare them to. You were looking at SaaS companies growing, what was it? 5X, 3X, 3X, 2X.
turns.zh: 如果你回看 2021 年，那些公司本身其实没那么有意思，只是我们没有别的东西可以拿来跟它们比。你看着那些 SaaS 公司增长，是多少来着？5 倍、3 倍、3 倍、2 倍。

turns.en: And everyone's like, that's best in class. And you would have companies with, you know, $8 million of SaaS revenue raising a billion dollar valuations. And they had very constrained tams. And you kind of had to look at these things for like a seven year timeline to get to 100 million of ARR.
turns.zh: 然后每个人都说，那是一流的（best in class）。你会有那种 SaaS 营收才 800 万美元、却以十亿美元估值融资的公司，而且它们的 TAM（潜在市场）非常受限。你几乎得用七年左右的时间线去看这些公司，才能到 1 亿美元 ARR。

turns.en: And that was what venture was back then. And that was exciting. And now you look at companies sitting on like, I kind of believe we've even got out of bed for those types of opportunities back then. In terms of the round structures, the volume of deals, people feeling the need that they need to keep up with the market is all very similar.
turns.zh: 那才是当时风险投资的样子，那很令人兴奋。现在你看着一些公司账上躺着——说实话我甚至觉得那种机会我们当年都懒得下床去做。就轮次结构、交易数量、人们觉得必须跟上市场的这种心态而言，都非常相似。

turns.en: In 2021, there was a period of time where if you pretty much ask every VC and even LPs about this similar situation, there's like a six month window in 2021 where VCs were just ripping checks.
turns.zh: 在 2021 年，有一段时间，你几乎去问每一个 VC、甚至 LP，都会听到类似的情况：2021 年有大约六个月的一个窗口期，那段时间 VC 就在疯狂开支票。

turns.en: And if you ask any of those VCs to look back at their portfolio for 2021 and that six month window, a lot of them are like, you know, we like to grab our heads and being like, what were we thinking doing all of those deals? I'm not saying we're at that point in the market today. Like we could be in 2019 and not 2021.
turns.zh: 如果你让那些 VC 回头看看他们在 2021 年、在那六个月窗口期里的投资组合，很多人会说，你知道吗，我们恨不得抱着头想，我们当时做那些交易到底是怎么想的？我并不是说我们今天已经到了市场的那个地步，比如我们现在可能更像是 2019 年，而不是 2021 年。

turns.en: But some of the things that I'm starting to see happen today in 2021 that was like public market investors trying to aggressively come into venture is very actively happening right now. How frantically people were trying to do deals back then versus how they're trying to do them now.
turns.zh: 但我今天开始看到的一些情况，在 2021 年也出现过，比如公开市场投资人试图激进地涌入风险投资，现在正在非常活跃地上演。当年人们做交易有多疯狂，对比现在他们做交易有多疯狂——

turns.en: Some of the things we started seeing near the late end of 2021 were companies getting term sheets very, very quickly and then term sheets getting pulled also very, very quickly or reneged or renegotiate in one way or another.
turns.zh: 我们在 2021 年接近尾声时开始看到的一些情况是，公司非常非常快地拿到条款清单（term sheet），然后条款清单又非常非常快地被撤回，或者被毁约、被以某种方式重新谈判。

turns.en: And the last six, seven, eight weeks, I've probably seen a larger amount of deals get renegotiated after being offered than I have since 2021. But the thing that's most dissimilar is kind of the enthusiasm around the companies.
turns.zh: 而在最近的六、七、八周里，我看到被报价后又被重新谈判的交易数量，可能比 2021 年以来的任何时候都多。但最不相似的地方，是围绕这些公司的那种热情。

turns.en: I don't think people were investing in companies in 2021 thinking that these companies were going to be category defining or be global scale companies within 18 to 24 months and that you're kind of just seeing in this market play out. You're having companies find product market fit at a faster rate than ever.
turns.zh: 我不认为 2021 年人们投资公司时，会认为这些公司将在 18 到 24 个月内成为品类定义者（category defining）或全球规模的公司，而这恰恰是你在这个市场里正在看到的。你正看到公司以比以往更快的速度找到产品市场契合（product market fit）。

turns.en: I'm looking at companies in my portfolio that I'm using very actively and I can't think of anything I invested in 2021 that I was using personally. turns.en: AI products or an tech products period and they become integrated as parts of their daily life. turns.zh: 对 AI 产品、或者说对任何科技产品都是如此，而这些产品却成了他们日常生活的一部分。所以我觉得这个市场里发生了一场巨大的范式转变，就是技术层面的入侵，人们真心相信：如果真有一个机会窗口是你不能坐视不理的，那就是当下这个时刻。

turns.en: Can you drill a level further down the stack which is to the LP side and the funds that are being raised. So this money comes from funds going into these companies at record paces and amounts. These these also have to raise money themselves from a group of LPs that have historically been the reason VC exists.
turns.zh: 你能不能再往这技术栈下面钻一层，也就是 LP（有限合伙人）这一侧，以及正在募集的这些基金。所以这些钱来自基金以创纪录的速度和金额投进这些公司。而这些基金自己也必须从一群 LP 那里募钱——正是这群 LP 历来是 VC 之所以存在的原因。

turns.en: Endowments and foundations and things like this. And like at some point it seems like what the market is doing is we're all spending so much money so quickly that the sources of capital themselves are starting to ask your questions.
turns.zh: 比如捐赠基金（endowment）、基金会（foundation）等等。而在某个点上，市场似乎正在做的是：我们所有人花钱花得太快太多，以至于资本的源头本身都开始提出问题。

turns.en: So when a venture capital fund typically goes out to raise capital they're raising for an 18 to 24 month window initial deployment period. That means that's the amount of cash they wanted to pull it into initial checks and then they reserve whatever they reserve for follow on to keep financing those companies to maintain their ownership.
turns.zh: 所以当一家风险投资基金出去募资时，他们募的是覆盖一个 18 到 24 个月窗口的初始投放期。也就是说，那是他们想用于开出初始支票的现金额，然后剩下的部分他们留作后续投资（follow-on）的储备，用来继续给这些公司融资、维持自己的持股比例。

turns.en: I think in the last 18 to 24 months the mega platform funds you guys hear about that are raising these record size funds have probably raised two to three times and that same 18 to 24 month window. So likely the pulling periods are about three X faster than they thought they would be.
turns.zh: 我觉得在过去 18 到 24 个月里，那些你听说过的、正在募集创纪录规模基金的超级平台基金（mega platform fund），很可能在同样的 18 到 24 个月窗口里已经募了两到三次。所以他们把钱投出去的速度大概是他们原本预想的三倍左右。

turns.en: Now what's interesting about that is when venture capital firms go out to raise these are the guys that have their pulse on the market better than anybody.
turns.zh: 现在有意思的地方在于，当风险投资公司出去募资时，这些人才是对市场脉搏把握得比谁都准的人。

turns.en: And they always raise an amount of capital that supports their portfolio construction model which means they want X number of bets with X number of out with X amount of ownership over X period of time typically 18 to 24 months.
turns.zh: 而且他们募的资本规模总是能支撑他们的组合构建模型，也就是说，他们想在 X 段时间里、以 X 比例的持股，押注 X 数量的赌注、拿到 X 数量的回报，通常这段时间是 18 到 24 个月。

turns.en: Every single one of the mega firms has dramatically underestimated how much capital they need to actually get that level of ownership in those companies over that window time which basically just means that there is a large number of companies they want to invest in and they thought they would.
turns.zh: 每一家超级机构（mega firm）都严重低估了他们要在那个时间窗口里、在那些公司中拿到那种持股比例所需要的资本量。这基本上就意味着，他们想投的公司数量比他们以为的要多得多。

turns.en: The price of those companies is higher than they thought it would be and the ownership they got in those companies in order to get that ownership they need to invest much more than they initially modeled out.
turns.zh: 那些公司的价格比他们以为的要高，而他们为了拿到想要的持股比例，在这些公司里需要投入的资本，也远远超过他们最初建模时的数字。

turns.en: So that's where you're seeing these guys not only come back to market sooner than they initially anticipated they're also coming back from much larger sums of capital.
turns.zh: 所以这就是为什么你会看到这些机构不仅比最初预期的更早回到市场，他们回来时募集的资本规模也大得多。

turns.en: So that's the most interesting thing that you're seeing in this market is LPs are kind of looking at these guys and realizing that there's two things that are happening that either maintain their ownership and these companies but they end up with way fewer shots on goal or they end up with way less ownership in these companies and end up with their same shots on goal.
turns.zh: 所以这就是你在这个市场里看到的最有意思的事情：LP 们看着这些机构，意识到正在发生两件事——要么维持他们在这些公司里的持股比例，但结果出手的次数（shots on goal）大大减少；要么他们在这些公司里的持股比例大大减少，而出手次数保持不变。

turns.en: The shots on goal basically is your hedge against not being a great picker you get the shots on goal that you need to have the number of winners you need to have a good venture capital fund.
turns.zh: 所谓出手次数，基本上就是你对自己不是个出色挑选者的对冲手段。你需要足够的出手次数，才能拥有足够数量的赢家，从而做出一只好的风险投资基金。

turns.en: But if you're not getting your ownership your upside will be capped in one way or another and then the alternative is you're like hey we actually need our ownership so we're going to just invest in fewer companies this vintage because we have to invest more capital in the companies who want to invest and get our own.
turns.zh: 但如果你拿不到你想要的持股比例，你的上行空间就会以某种方式被封顶。那么另一种选择就是：嘿，我们确实需要保住持股比例，所以这一期（vintage）我们就只投更少的公司，因为我们必须在想投的公司上投入更多资本，才能拿到我们想要的持股。

turns.en: And that aspect just need to be a better picker but you could still produce outsize returns because you're getting the core positions in the companies that you want core exposure to from an LP perspective.
turns.zh: 而那样一来，你就只需要成为一个更出色的挑选者，但你仍然能产生超额回报，因为你在那些你想要核心敞口的公司里拿到了核心仓位——这是从 LP 的角度说的。

turns.en: I think those guys were expecting dramatically more liquidity at this point in the cycle than they've actually gotten and it's actually funny because you look at LPs that had 35 to 50% of their exposure and the venture capital but if you actually put out a layer back it's not 30 to 40% of their 50% of their AUM and venture capital that's 30 to 50% of their AUM and like three to four companies.
turns.zh: 我觉得那些人原本预期在这个周期的这个时点能拿到的流动性，远比他们实际拿到的要多。而且有意思的是，你会看到那些把 35% 到 50% 敞口放在风险投资里的 LP，但如果你真去剥开一层看，那不是他们 AUM 的 30% 到 40%，也不是他们 AUM 的 50% 放在 VC 里——那是他们 AUM 的 30% 到 50% 集中在三到四家公司上。

turns.en: And that's SpaceX, Amthropic and OpenAI and Databricks and a number of companies like that. Those are the names that need to generate liquidity for these guys to get their exposure levels to the asset class down.
turns.zh: 而那就是 SpaceX、Anthropic、OpenAI、Databricks 以及诸如此类的一批公司。正是这些名字需要产生流动性，才能让这些 LP 把对该资产类别的敞口水平降下来。

turns.en: It doesn't actually have to do with all of these companies you're hearing about. There's just a few companies that really moved the needle for all of these LPs. And if you're an LP that wasn't in a fund that had a lot of exposure to SpaceX you haven't gotten any liquidity.
turns.zh: 这其实跟你听到的所有这些公司都没什么关系。真正为所有这些 LP 撬动局面的就那么几家公司。而如果你是一个 LP，你投的基金里没有大量 SpaceX 的敞口，那你就没拿到任何流动性。

turns.en: Basically the LPs that are going to generate meaningful liquidity are the ones that have exposure to funds that have meaningful exposure to those companies. Outside of exposure to those companies LPs aren't getting much liquidity back at all.
turns.zh: 基本上，那些能产生有意义流动性的 LP，是那些对有大量敞口在这些公司上的基金有敞口的 LP。除了对这些公司的敞口之外，LP 根本没拿回多少流动性。

turns.en: I think that puts the funds that don't have LPs that have exposure to those companies in a position where they're trying to actually extract new sources of capital for their companies because a lot of the LPs are limited on cash. The traditional LPs that you and I would think about as the guys who fund the venture capital ecosystem.
turns.zh: 我觉得这让那些 LP 没有上述公司敞口的基金，处在一个尴尬的位置：他们试图为自己的公司挖出新的资本来源，因为很多 LP 现金有限。那些传统的、你我会想到的、为整个风险投资生态系统提供资金的 LP——

turns.en: Could you give an example of a fund again without naming it and rough numbers not the Pacific of the sort of history and the accelerated pace of deployment? I know one fund that raised two and a half billion dollars and started deploying in July and told me they're going to be back in March and January.
turns.zh: 你能不能举一个基金的例子，同样不用点名、只给个大概数字，讲讲这种历史以及投放节奏的加速？我知道有一只基金募了 25 亿美元，7 月开始投放，然后告诉我他们明年 3 月、1 月就要回来（再募）了。

turns.en: I know of another fund where my LPs told me they gave them three billion dollars nine months ago and now they're back looking for five billion dollars. They'll get it. These guys are all great managers and they'll get the numbers they're looking for but that's the intensity of the pace.
turns.zh: 我还知道另一只基金，我的 LP 告诉我，他们九个月前给了那只基金 30 亿美元，现在它又回来找 50 亿美元了。他们会募到的。这些都是很棒的基金管理人，他们会拿到想要的数字，但这就体现了节奏的强度。

turns.en: The other thing that's really interesting about this market is not only do these guys need more money quicker than they thought they needed it. But now it's actually certain have ripple effects so the companies that are getting their term sheets in terms of when they actually get the capital that they were committed to.
turns.zh: 这个市场里另一件非常有意思的事是，这些机构不仅比他们以为的更快需要更多钱，而且现在这还会产生某种连锁反应。所以那些拿到条款清单的公司，在实际拿到被承诺的资本的时间点上——

turns.en: So I'm seeing companies in the last eight to 12 weeks and this is the first time I started to see this in the cycle where the VCs are giving them term sheets and saying, Hey, we want to put $150 million in your company. Is it okay if we fund it in like mid-January, which is three months from now and Founders like wait a second,
turns.zh: 所以在最近的八到十二周里，这是我在这个周期里第一次开始看到这种情况：VC 给公司发条款清单，说嘿，我们想往你公司投 1.5 亿美元，我们大概 1 月中旬打款行不行？——那是三个月之后。创始人会说等一下，

turns.en: when you need three months to fund and they're like, no, no, we're good for it and they are all the money in our current fund is already committed to existing companies and we're in the middle of closing a new fund. But by the time we get all those docs in and on board it and we got our capital has already set up.
turns.zh: 你们居然需要三个月才能打款？他们会说不不，我们没问题的，我们现在这只基金里所有的钱都已经承诺给现有公司了，而我们正在关闭一只新基金。但等我们把所有文件走完、把新基金 onboard 进来、资本都到位——

turns.en: It's going to be like mid-January before we fund. We had another company that got a $50 million term sheet from one VC firm and the VC was going to do 40 out of the 50. And they said we could wire five million upon closing and we need another eight to 10 weeks to fund the remainder of our commitments.
turns.zh: 那差不多要到 1 月中旬才能打款。我们还有另一家公司，从一家 VC 机构那里拿到了 5000 万美元的条款清单，那家 VC 打算在 5000 万里出 4000 万。他们说我们可以在交割时先汇 500 万美元，剩下的承诺部分我们还需要八到十周才能到位。

turns.en: So that's kind of interesting in terms of like these guys are committing deals before they even have the money to finance and they'll get the money. But it just draws attention to the pace that these things are really getting deployed to step all the way back.
turns.zh: 所以就很有意思——从这些机构在还没拿到融资的钱之前就先承诺交易这一点来看，他们最终会拿到钱的。但这恰恰凸显了这些东西被投放出去的节奏有多快。把视角整个拉远来看，

turns.en: This seems furious and unsustainable and maybe understandable given that it's funding the most interesting technology build out. Any of us will ever see or in human history or whatever. But the Anthropic S1 came out which makes an interesting day to be having this discussion.
turns.zh: 这看起来又疯狂又不可持续，考虑到它资助的是我们任何人此生、或者说人类历史上所能见到的最有意思的技术建设，也许又情有可原。但 Anthropic 的 S-1（招股书）出来了，这让今天成了进行这场讨论的一个有意思的日子。

turns.en: The most glaring stat in that thing is that they've raised 140 billion and they've spent 10 of that and they have 132 billion on the balance sheet. That's pretty amazing that they've earned $10 billion of cash. Forget about all the future commitments and the liabilities and all these things for just a moment.
turns.zh: 那份文件里最扎眼的一个数据是，他们已经融了 1400 亿美元，花掉了其中的 100 亿，账上还有 1320 亿现金。这相当惊人——他们攒下了 100 亿美元的现金。先别管所有那些未来的承诺、负债等等这些东西。

turns.en: But $10 billion of cash to get to the revenue numbers that they're at with 85% gross margins is unbelievable. Does all this make you wonder if we need some innovation in financial products? It seems like when you boil down why everyone needs all this stuff the answer is always just compute.
turns.zh: 但用 100 亿美元的现金烧出他们现在这样的营收数字，而且毛利率还有 85%，这真是难以置信。这一切是否让你觉得，我们需要在金融产品上做一些创新？看起来，当你把为什么每个人都需要所有这些东西归结到根上，答案永远只是算力（compute）。

turns.en: It just makes me wonder are we trying to solve a very modern problem with what's become an antiquated instrument or style given this psychotic behavior. Yes and no. There are no shortage of new debt vehicles to finance growth and companies. I think GC has their customer value, customer value fund.
turns.zh: 这就不禁让我想，鉴于这种近乎疯狂的行为，我们是不是在用一个已经过时的工具或方式，去解决一个非常现代的问题？既是也不是。为增长和公司融资的新型债务工具并不短缺。我觉得 GC 有他们的客户价值基金（customer value fund）。

turns.en: If you could prove that for every $10 million that unlocks $30 million of revenue will give you the money to finance that. I guess that sort of makes my point though. That thing's been from a product perspective enormously successful. They've raised tons of money if you think it has a product. It's done really well.
turns.zh: 如果你能证明每投入 1000 万美元就能解锁 3000 万美元的营收，他们就会给你钱来为这个融资。我想这在某种程度上正好印证了我的观点。那个东西从产品角度看已经取得了巨大的成功，他们募了大量资金。如果你觉得它是个产品，那它做得非常好。

turns.en: What I'm wondering is do we need way more things like that for each type of spending that's happening in these companies? Lots of which is panic buying or reserving of compute ahead of anticipated demand.
turns.zh: 我在想的是，对于这些公司里发生的每一种支出类型，我们是不是需要远比这更多的此类工具？其中很多支出，是在预期需求到来之前，恐慌性地抢购或预订算力。

turns.en: Some of these personal agent companies are thinking about how much money they're going to need to spend to grow to the daily active user counts they need. I think there are vehicles that are emerging. There are some VC firms that are financing companies with compute as opposed to cash.
turns.zh: 其中一些个人智能体（personal agent）公司，正在盘算他们要成长到所需的日活跃用户数（DAU），得花掉多少钱。我觉得有一些新的融资载体正在出现。有一些 VC 机构在用算力、而不是现金来给公司融资。

turns.en: And for a lot of the founders we talk to that's actually more attractive. I like if you bring this compute instead of cash you guaranteed your allocation this round because we're going to take this money and spend it on compute regardless. I think there's some people doing that but then you have to go secure the compute.
turns.zh: 而且对我们交流的很多创始人来说，那其实更有吸引力。就像如果你带来的是算力而不是现金，那你这一轮的额度就有保证了，因为反正我们会把这笔钱拿去花在算力上。我觉得有些人在这么做，但接着你就得去把算力搞到手。

turns.en: And you have to make sure you're getting good pricing on the compute. And then it's a little complicated in terms of do you give them the compute and perpetuity? Do you have the compute for one training run? How many times can you recycle that same amount of compute to actually make up for the amount of capital you have deployed?
turns.zh: 而且你得确保你拿到的算力价格不错。然后这就有点复杂了：你是永久给他们算力，还是只给一次训练运行（training run）的算力？同一批算力你能循环利用多少次，才能真正抵消你投入的资本量？

turns.en: Like can you recycle the amount of compute you have three times two times one time? How much do things actually get degraded over time? I think there's a lot of complexities in that.
turns.zh: 比如，你手上的算力能循环用三次、两次、还是一次？这些东西随时间实际上会贬值多少？我觉得这里面有很多复杂之处。

turns.en: I haven't seen much else getting new capital structures to get widely adopted in Silicon Valley is complex and challenging because VCs by default like their companies having clean equity that don't have unique covenants that can put the company in a tricky spot if they don't think about them.
turns.zh: 我还没看到太多新的资本结构能在硅谷被广泛采用，因为这既复杂又有挑战——VC 天生就喜欢自己的公司拥有干净的股权（clean equity），不喜欢那些独特的契约条款（covenant），因为如果考虑不周，这些条款可能让公司陷入棘手处境。

turns.en: I think by default most founders are like we just want to clean equity deal where we know what we gave away what we got in return. GC's value creation fund is doing great now but I think in the early couple years of it was a very significant like education process why this is a good product why it should read for you.
turns.zh: 我觉得大多数创始人天生就想要一笔干净的股权交易，清楚地知道自己让渡了什么、换回了什么。GC 的价值创造基金（value creation fund）现在做得很好，但我记得它头几年是个非常重大的教育过程——要向大家解释为什么这是个好产品、为什么它对你有意义。

turns.en: Because founders usually for anything capital related rely back on their VCs for opinions on whether this is a good capital source and VCs historically don't like venture debt products. So they give you a million reasons why you shouldn't do it.
turns.zh: 因为创始人通常在任何跟资本相关的事情上，都会回头依赖他们的 VC，去判断这是不是个好的资本来源。而 VC 历来不喜欢风险债务（venture debt）产品，所以他们会给你一百万个不该这么做的理由。

turns.en: And then I think the other side needs to give you the million reasons why you should do it because it does make sense because it is a new product created for this day and age adventure capital.
turns.zh: 然后我觉得另一边需要给你一百万个应该这么做的理由，因为它确实说得通——它是为当今这个时代的风险投资打造的一款新产品。
